flashcards.front_question: Why do different individuals have different developmental goals?
flashcards.back_answer: Different people have different developmental goals because their life situations, socio-economic backgrounds, and immediate needs differ. What is progress for one person may not be progress for another, and can sometimes even be destructive to others.

flashcards.front_question: Give an example of a developmental goal that creates conflict between two groups of people.
flashcards.back_answer: Industrialists wanting large hydroelectric dams to obtain more electricity vs. indigenous tribal communities whose land and livelihoods are submerged by dam construction.

flashcards.front_question: Besides monetary income, what non-material goals are essential for human development?
flashcards.back_answer: Non-material goals include equal treatment, personal freedom, physical security, respect from others, non-discrimination, safe working conditions, and work-life balance.

flashcards.front_question: How does the World Bank compare and classify different countries in its World Development Reports?
flashcards.back_answer: The World Bank classifies countries based on Per Capita Income (Total National Income divided by Total Population).

flashcards.front_question: What are the Per Capita Income thresholds used by the World Bank (2021) to categorize rich and low-income countries?
flashcards.back_answer: Rich/High-income countries have a Per Capita Income above USD 49,300 per annum. Low-income countries have a Per Capita Income of USD 2,500 per annum or less (India's PCI was USD 2,370 in 2021).

flashcards.front_question: Why is Per Capita Income considered an inadequate metric for evaluating total national development?
flashcards.back_answer: Per Capita Income hides income distribution disparities (wealth concentration among elites), ignores health metrics (Infant Mortality Rate), educational achievements (literacy, school attendance), and excludes environmental quality and security.

flashcards.front_question: When comparing Haryana and Kerala, why does Kerala rank higher in overall development despite having lower Per Capita Income?
flashcards.back_answer: Kerala has far better human development indicators: Infant Mortality Rate of 7 per 1,000 live births (vs. Haryana's 30), a Literacy Rate of 94% (vs. Haryana's 80%), and a Net Attendance Ratio of 83% (vs. Haryana's 61%), owing to strong public health and education systems.

flashcards.front_question: What is Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)?
flashcards.back_answer: The number of children that die before completing one year of age as a proportion of 1,000 live children born in that specific year.

flashcards.front_question: What is Net Attendance Ratio?
flashcards.back_answer: The total number of children of age group 14 and 15 years attending school as a percentage of total number of children in the same age group.

flashcards.front_question: Which international organization publishes the Human Development Report, and what three key dimensions does it measure?
flashcards.back_answer: The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). It evaluates health (life expectancy), education (mean and expected years of schooling), and standard of living (Gross National Income per capita).

flashcards.front_question: How is Body Mass Index (BMI) calculated, and what do its cutoff values indicate for adults?
flashcards.back_answer: BMI = Weight in kilograms / (Height in meters) squared. A BMI under 18.5 indicates undernourishment/malnutrition, while a BMI of 25 or above indicates an overweight status.

flashcards.front_question: What is Sustainable Development, and why is it crucial for economic planning?
flashcards.back_answer: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, avoiding resource depletion and ecological degradation.

flashcards.front_question: Distinguish between renewable and exhaustible natural resources using examples from India's development context.
flashcards.back_answer: Renewable resources (e.g., groundwater) replenish naturally, but over-exploitation (like groundwater pumping in Punjab/Western UP) leads to water table collapse. Exhaustible resources (e.g., crude oil reserves) have fixed global stocks and will be depleted permanently if overused.

flashcards.front_question: Define the Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary sectors of an economy.
flashcards.back_answer: Primary: Exploitation/extraction of natural resources (agriculture, mining, fishing). Secondary: Processing and manufacturing raw materials into industrial goods (cotton to yarn, sugar cane to sugar). Tertiary: Providing support services for production (transport, banking, IT, trade).

flashcards.front_question: How is Gross Domestic Product (GDP) calculated, and why are intermediate goods excluded?
flashcards.back_answer: GDP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a financial year. Intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double counting, as their value is already included in the final product's market price.

flashcards.front_question: What unique structural anomaly characterized the sectoral shift in India's GDP versus employment between 1973 and 2014?
flashcards.back_answer: While the Tertiary sector's share of GDP grew dramatically to over 50%, the share of employment did not shift proportionally out of Agriculture—leaving over 44% of the labor force stuck in the Primary sector contributing under 16% of GDP.

flashcards.front_question: What is Disguised Unemployment (Underemployment), and in which sector is it most prominent in India?
flashcards.back_answer: A situation where more workers are engaged in an activity than required, so individual marginal productivity is zero. Removing extra workers does not reduce total output. It is most prominent in smallholder family agriculture.

flashcards.front_question: What is MGNREGA 2005, and what key statutory guarantee does it offer rural households?
flashcards.back_answer: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 guarantees 100 days of wage employment per year to rural households willing to do unskilled manual work, providing an unemployment allowance if work is not assigned within 15 days.

flashcards.front_question: Contrast the working conditions of the Organised sector with the Unorganised sector.
flashcards.back_answer: Organised: Registered with government, strict adherence to laws, fixed working hours, paid leave, minimum wages, provident fund, medical benefits, and job security. Unorganised: Unregistered, low/irregular wages, long hours, no paid leave, no medical safety, and vulnerable to arbitrary dismissal.

flashcards.front_question: Why is Public Sector involvement essential for infrastructure development despite the presence of a Private Sector?
flashcards.back_answer: Public Sector enterprises prioritize social welfare over profit, undertaking heavy capital investments with long gestation periods (highways, railways, power generation, public health, education) that private companies will not fund at affordable rates.

flashcards.front_question: What is the 'Double Coincidence of Wants', and how does money eliminate this problem?
flashcards.back_answer: A situation in a barter economy where two traders each possess a commodity desired by the other. Money acts as an intermediate medium of exchange, allowing buyers and sellers to conduct separate transactions without needing matching barter desires.

flashcards.front_question: Why is paper currency accepted as a valid medium of exchange in India?
flashcards.back_answer: Because currency notes and coins are authorized by the Central Government and issued exclusively by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), making refusal of rupee payments illegal.

flashcards.front_question: What are Demand Deposits, and how do cheques facilitate cashless money transfer?
flashcards.back_answer: Deposits in bank accounts withdrawable on demand. A cheque is a written instruction directing the bank to pay a specific sum from the drawer's account to the payee's account directly.

flashcards.front_question: How do commercial banks generate profit from the deposits they hold?
flashcards.back_answer: Banks retain ~15% of deposits as liquid cash reserves for daily withdrawals and extend the remaining 85% as loans. Bank profit is the spread between higher interest rates charged on loans and lower interest rates paid to depositors.

flashcards.front_question: Contrast a Virtuous Credit Situation with a Vicious Credit Situation (Debt Trap) using examples from the text.
flashcards.back_answer: Virtuous Credit (Salim): Working capital loan allows fulfillment of shoe orders, generating profits that clear the loan. Vicious Credit (Swapna): Loan taken for groundnut farming fails due to pest damage, forcing borrowing at high interest rates that compel land sale to pay off debt.

flashcards.front_question: What are the key elements included under 'Terms of Credit'?
flashcards.back_answer: Interest rate, collateral security, documentation required, and mode/schedule of repayment.

flashcards.front_question: Compare Formal and Informal sources of credit in India.
flashcards.back_answer: Formal (Banks/Cooperatives): Supervised by RBI, reasonable interest rates (8-12%), requires collateral and documentation. Informal (Moneylenders/Traders/Landlords): Unregulated, exorbitant interest rates (36-60%), coercive recovery, usually requires no formal collateral.

flashcards.front_question: How do Self-Help Groups (SHGs) help rural poor women overcome the lack of collateral?
flashcards.back_answer: SHGs pool weekly savings from 15-20 members to extend micro-loans. Regular savings make the group eligible for collateral-free bank loans because group peer responsibility guarantees repayment.

flashcards.front_question: What is a Multinational Corporation (MNC)?
flashcards.back_answer: A company that owns or controls production facilities for goods or services in more than one country.

flashcards.front_question: How do MNCs interlink production across different countries?
flashcards.back_answer: MNCs interlink production by establishing joint ventures with local firms, acquiring local domestic enterprises (e.g. Cargill buying Parakh Foods), placing sub-contracting orders with small producers, and deploying global supply chains.

flashcards.front_question: What key technological innovations accelerated the pace of globalisation in logistics and communication?
flashcards.back_answer: Containerization (standardized sea/rail containers cutting port handling time and transport cost) and Information & Communication Technology (satellite communication, internet, digital file transfer for service exports).

flashcards.front_question: What is Liberalisation, and when did India adopt major trade liberalisation policies?
flashcards.back_answer: Liberalisation is the removal of government restrictions, import tariffs, and trade barriers. India implemented major liberalisation reforms in 1991.

flashcards.front_question: What role does the World Trade Organisation (WTO) play, and what is a primary criticism of its operations?
flashcards.back_answer: The WTO establishes rules for global free trade. A major criticism is that developed nations force developing nations to eliminate trade barriers while retaining massive domestic agricultural subsidies themselves.

flashcards.front_question: Why has the impact of globalisation been uneven across different socio-economic groups in India?
flashcards.back_answer: Benefited urban wealthy consumers (greater choice, lower prices), large Indian MNCs (Infosys, Tata), and IT professionals, but severely damaged small domestic manufacturers (capacitors, toys shutting down) and forced workers into flexible, insecure unorganized employment.

flashcards.front_question: What are Special Economic Zones (SEZs), and why are they created?
flashcards.back_answer: Designated industrial zones with world-class infrastructure, 5-year tax holidays, and flexible labor laws established by governments to attract foreign direct investment (FDI).

flashcards.front_question: What historical factor led to the rise of the consumer movement in India during the 1960s?
flashcards.back_answer: Widespread consumer discontent regarding food shortages, hoarding, black marketing, under-weighing, and adulteration of food grains and edible oils.

flashcards.front_question: What is COPRA, and when is National Consumers Day celebrated in India?
flashcards.back_answer: Consumer Protection Act enacted in 1986 (updated 2019). National Consumers Day is celebrated every year on December 24.

flashcards.front_question: List the six statutory Consumer Rights granted under COPRA.
flashcards.back_answer: 1. Right to Safety, 2. Right to Information, 3. Right to Choose, 4. Right to be Heard / Representation, 5. Right to Seek Redressal, 6. Right to Consumer Education.

flashcards.front_question: How does the Right to Information (RTI) Act 2005 empower citizens in relation to both market products and government services?
flashcards.back_answer: For goods: Mandates package disclosures (ingredients, MRP, batch, expiry). For government: Enables citizens to demand official records on public work delays, administrative decisions, and public utility operations.

flashcards.front_question: Name the three-tier quasi-judicial redressal commission structure established under COPRA and their 2019 monetary claim thresholds.
flashcards.back_answer: 1. District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (claims up to ₹1 crore). 2. State Consumer Commission (claims ₹1 crore to ₹10 crore). 3. National Consumer Commission (claims above ₹10 crore).

flashcards.front_question: Identify the official quality certification marks for electrical goods, agricultural produce, and gold jewelry in India.
flashcards.back_answer: Electrical/industrial goods: ISI Mark (BIS). Agricultural produce: Agmark. Gold jewelry: Hallmark (BIS).

flashcards.front_question: Why is insisting on a cash receipt/bill critical when making consumer purchases?
flashcards.back_answer: A cash receipt acts as legal documentary proof of purchase required by Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions to file claims for replacement or compensation.
